millimeter-wave systems have received little attention in the design of hybrid precoders. To fill this gap, we develop the first integrated design of analog transmit precoders and digital receive combiners for multicasting in mmWave systems, with each device having multiple phases and multiple antennas. By combining semidefinite relaxation, alternating optimization and Cholesky decomposition, we sequentially optimize the digital and analog components at the transmitter and receivers. The proposed method leads to significant performance improvements. Notably, with two receive antennas, we see an average reduction of $ 16.8\% $ in the transmit power needed per message and a rise of $ 60\% $ in the information successfully received. Simulation experiments demonstrate that the designed precoder system functions nearly as well as a fully-digital version even in the presence of difficult transmission conditions.

Our study examines how to effectively manage the flow of service requests across an NDN-based network, considering the varying levels of availability for each service on individual nodes. driving and drone operation could benefit from distributed machine learning (DML) over dynamically changing networks. Yet, standard weighted arithmetic mean aggregation in current DML systems may lead to considerable model inaccuracies and slow convergence speeds over fluctuating networks. In this study, in order to enhance model reliability and performance in such scenarios, we introduce a new family of nonlinear aggregation functions. Our nonlinear aggregation function family is based on the generated versus observed data discrepancy principle. We utilize one member of this family, the log-sum-exp function, to devise a new nonlinear aggregation function. Our results indicate that the proposed log-sum-exp aggregator has a higher convergence rate than the weighted arithmetic mean aggregator in distributed learning applications.

made it easy for software developers to share and reuse code across various repositories, often employing clone-and-own or forking techniques. As a result, it has become crucial to effectively maintain these shared files, especially in keeping them updated to the most recent version of a shared file. This contrasts with previous approaches, where our proposal of meta-maintenance - tracking the evolution of a single file across multiple repositories to identify potential maintenance opportunities, can now be achieved. In order to accomplish this, we first analyzed 49,099 repositories from GitHub and Bitbucket, discovering that 24% of all repositories contain files that have been shared or duplicated through clone-and-own or forking methods. This suggests that a targeted software maintenance strategy that incorporates meta-maintenance could significantly improve efficiency. Additionally, we also found other meaningful insights, which will be discussed in our study.

on the mass distribution of black holes across various sizes, spanning from the mass of stars to supermassive entities. Previous research revealed that the mass range of stellar-mass black holes can be described through a normal distribution. This follow-up investigates the probability density function describing smaller black hole masses, referred to as intermediate-mass black holes. Using the hypothesis that all short-lived cosmic rays with exceptional energies are generated by the decay of intermediate-mass black holes, researchers have been able to calculate the number of such black holes in the early universe. This calculation yields a comfortable fit between theoretical estimates and existing data from radio astronomy surveys regarding intermediate-mass black hole existence. Consequently, it is proposed that the mass distribution of intermediate-mass black holes follows a broken power law. Combining this finding with the normal distribution representation of stellar-mass black holes, it is suggested that the mass distribution of all cosmic black holes may follow a structurally consistent pattern.

Two of the 'linear' co-adding algorithms tested yield consistent results identical to those obtained through traditional linear co-adding involving transmission maps. These algorithms are named linear co-adding and it's based on an average over an area. The transmission map average algorithm is specifically suited to situations where the point spread function doesn't change significantly. We propose an interpretation where Fisher's average excess and average effect are intended to represent a fundamental distinction between statistical correlation and causality, and according to this understanding, the average effect specifically measures the weighted outcomes of a homogeneous population after controlling for differences. This perspective implies that the average excess, which represents uncontrolled influences, is inherently linked with confounding variables, whereas the average effect, which represents effective influences, is connected with causality. The semi-supervised pseudo-labeling method is often employed to mitigate this issue, which aims to supplement the training set with high-confidence, pseudo-labeled nodes in a self-training cycle. Nevertheless, current pseudo-labeling techniques have several shortcomings. Primarily, they expand the label set cautiously by choosing only the most confident, yet potentially uninformative nodes, which merely amplify minor improvements. Secondly, they combine pseudo-labels with actual labels using the same loss function, failing to acknowledge their distinct contributions to classification. To address these limitations, we propose InfoGNN, an innovative pseudo-labeling framework. InfoGNN focuses on labeling nodes with the greatest informative value rather than mere confidence. To do this, InfoGNN utilizes both local and global information to calculate the entropy of candidate nodes and selects those with lower entropy for labeling. Furthermore, to counterbalance the influence of pseudo-labels and actual labels, InfoGNN utilizes a multi-loss weighting strategy during combined training. Experimental evaluations on six graph datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method.

Through the application of duality theory, this complex problem is transformed into a more manageable form, allowing for the successful implementation of various resource allocation schemes. Specifically, this research demonstrates that solving a dual problem with a specific constraint related to relay allocation leads to optimal results for both user maximization and system optimization. Consequently, novel adaptive power allocation and scheduling algorithms are introduced that take into account the optimal relay allocation. Furthermore, this research successfully shows the feasibility of these proposed algorithms through both theoretical and simulation-based analysis.

Braitenberg vehicles can manifest complex, unpredictable movements. Employing a robot design inspired by the work of Stewart, the experiments demonstrate that these entities can display a range of erratic movements. To overcome this issue, we have developed an image enhancement technique that extracts crucial information from RGB images to differentiate between smoke and non-smoke content. we've found that titanium in barium titanate experiences a significant shift in its atomic size during the material's phase change from a cubic to a rhombohedra structure. Our research introduces a set of conditions known as 'i-mixing properties' that facilitate average-case evaluations for a broad range of algorithms, including k-means and Gaussian mixture distribution-based clustering methods. By assuming data comes from a smooth, high-dimensional space with sufficient dimensionality, our analysis provides optimal worst-case and near-worst-case results comparable to those achieved under uniform distribution assumptions. Our findings refine existing results, providing detailed information about convergence rates, and can be applied to a broad range of clustering algorithms. Additionally, our research provides approximate performance bounds for first-order algorithm variants. To demonstrate the i-mixing property's utility, we establish a precise performance guarantee for the kmn algorithm, a direct algorithmic counterpart to the k-means method. Our results show the superiority of hyperbolic loss functions over quadratic loss for optimal performance and the potential for compensating losses in challenging clustering scenarios. Our research also provides a precise performance guarantee for the clustermix algorithm, an algorithm designed to robustly cluster data despite adversarial noise. Our findings reveal the efficient robust clustering capability of this algorithm under mild assumptions and its potential applicability in a range of generalized clustering scenarios. Ultimately, the i-mixing property can be utilized to analyze any clustering algorithm assuming data comes from a smooth, high-dimensional space.

For example, in the medical field, a treatment guideline might not cover all co-factors a patient can have and therefore supplementary restrictions might need to be considered. Sometimes, these constraints may conflict with existing guidelines, requiring either the guidelines or the constraints to be violated. To address this issue, we suggest a solution to monitor hybrid process definitions expressed through a combination of (data-aware) Petri nets and temporal logic rules. During the process execution, the monitoring system can handle all specifications at once by providing violation reports according to a chosen strategy, either by violating the guidelines, the constraints, or a combination of both. Our monitoring solution works by first reducing the given specifications to a standardized format, called marked graphs, and then using AI solvers to determine possible violations. These AI solers are based on our own method called Temporal Fitting. The monitoring method has been tested with several example processes, showing that it can handle semi-automatically generate violation reports which also take data variables into account.

Yet, its embedded nature in Haskell hinders the development of a formal semantics and restricts the type system. The absence of linear types in Haskell makes it simple to write quantum state-cloning violating code. The Proto-Quipper family addresses this issue through research languages alternative to Haskell, specifically Linear Quipper and its predecessors. This paper comprehends Linear Quipper into the existing Quipper family by integrating it with the existing, embedded, yet mutable version of the language. The study also establishes a linear algebraic mean calculus as a denotational semantics for Linear Quipper and proves its correspondence with a proposed operational semantics. The results show that mutable references do not compromise linear consistency in Quipper.

While the second eigenvalue lies on the periphery of a semicircular distribution, influenced by the parameter p, the first eigenvalue is characterised by a distinct, isolated Gaussian distribution, leading to a diverse set of critical behaviors and finite-size scaling effects. Our computational analysis combined with theoretical arguments demonstrates how the convergence of the first two eigenvalues in the thermodynamic limit leads to a divergent power-law. To capture the complexity of critical behaviors, we have derived a scaling law describing a set of universal exponents governing the fluctuation of extreme eigenvalues. Our work may offer a simplified and practical approach to study critical phenomena in intricate systems and their associated inverse problems, initially inspired by the investigation into the critical behavior of a random matrix model involving a divergent power-law.

DNA sequences is a critical yet computationally complex task within the genomics pipeline. Due to the rapidly expanding genomic dataset, high-performance and scalable approaches are essential for managing the increased computational demands. A novel, parallel algorithm is proposed, utilizing a graph representation and sparse matrices, that tackles genome assembly through graph reduction. By integrating graph and sparse matrix data structures to represent edge relationships between overlapping DNA sequences, the algorithm efficiently identifies and merges sequential DNA segments. Key components, including graph and matrix creation, contraction, and node merging, are discussed and demonstrated to achieve optimal scalability with state-of-the-art parallel processing architectures.

Our study proposes an improved logistic equation with a clearer biological foundation based on cell population dynamics, incorporating discrete and distributed delay terms. The model's global dynamics are fully analyzed and proven to result in all feasible nontrivial solutions converging to the stable positive equilibrium. The main evidence for the model relies on persistence theory, a comparison principle, and a $L^2$-perturbation technique. Utilizing local invariant manifolds, a singular heteroclinic orbit is constructed, linking the unstable zero and stable positive equilibrium. The model is found to exhibit complex, global dynamics where transient, oscillating patterns persist over long durations, and we discuss their relevance to other delay-based logistic models.

Recent research has developed a point process depth by incorporating a weighted product of two terms - one representing the depth of process magnitude, and the other describing the temporal occurrence of events given that magnitude. The second component is challenging due to the complex nature of event timings and thus far, methods like Gaussian and Dirichlet distributions have been used despite being oversimplified representations. Consequently, current methods fail to account for the actual underlying pattern of events in the process and thus lack clarity and versatility when dealing with intricate patterns. In order to tackle this issue, a new method based on the distribution of events via the Isometric Log-Ratio (ILR) transformation is proposed, focusing on the inter-event intervals. The ILR depth measure is initially defined for a uniform Poisson process using a transformed space and its applicability is later extended to all point processes using time-rescaling techniques. The ILR depth's efficiency is showcased via simulations involving Poisson and non-Poisson processes, highlighting its superiority over existing approaches, while its theoretical properties and asymptotic analysis are also meticulously investigated. Ultimately, a practical case study confirms the effectiveness of the proposed ILR depth method.

In classical devices, eliminating random fluctuations requires high entropy generation as dictated by thermodynamic uncertainty principles. Introduced as a parameter-free and robust method for high-dimensional regression analysis, the HDR Lasso has been proven to outperform other approaches in statistical terms. Building on the adaptive sieving strategy from the Exclusive Lasso problem, we introduce a novel HDR Lasso solution that takes full advantage of the problem's sparse nature, solving smaller subproblems in each iteration through the proximal point algorithm. intelligence have positioned it as a key tool for addressing environmental concerns, primarily reducing greenhouse gas emissions. However, researchers have lately come to recognize that increasingly complex AI models require substantial amounts of energy to train, thereby contributing to the very emissions they are intended to mitigate. To date, no thorough examination of the full scope of the environmental effects of using AI to address environmental problems (a phenomenon referred to as AI for Green) has been undertaken, focusing exclusively on greenhouse gas emissions. In this study, we seek to address this gap by exploring the broader environmental implications of AI for Green through an established framework that encompasses multiple critical factors. Initially, we categorize and evaluate the environmental influence of AI solutions to environmental issues into four distinct areas: data-driven analysis, AI-optimized solutions, AI-enabled services, and AI product development. Subsequently, we illustrate the application of our framework by conducting a comprehensive analysis of one AI for Green sub-field: weather forecasting. In doing so, we identify both promising opportunities and significant challenges toward minimizing the environmental impact of AI for Green. Ultimately, we pinpoint key research areas that require further attention in this domain.

We have developed a model that captures how individuals with limited confidence in their judgments form opinions based on their personal relationships. We considered scenarios with one and two distinct aspects of opinions, and found that our framework consistently leads to the separation of agents into two distinct groups, characterized by distinct opinion sets. Depending on the level of trust, these groups either develop uniform views or multiple distinct perspectives within each group emerge. In the case of opinions based on a single dimension, our model leads to a stable state, whereas introducing multiple dimensions leads to dynamics that resemble opinion ecology, with agents organizing into groups with shared views on multiple issues. Our results suggest that trust can lead to the stabilization of fragile social systems, allowing for more complex structures to exist.

Inside the event horizon, this hair acts as a local pure scalar condensate, essentially a non-trivial solution to the Einstein-Yukawa theory equations, with the scalar field exhibiting a Cauchy surface instability. We dug deeper into the stability of the Cauchy surface and found that it's fundamentally tied to the instability of the universal binding curve in the phase diagram of the Einstein-Yukawa model, particularly at its point of equilibrium. Additionally, we explored how the stability of the Cauchy surface changes when the black holes collide with scalar "hair" particles, which caused the instability to grow stronger under these conditions. Although the stability of the Cauchy surface remains an open question for certain types of scalar fields, our analysis suggests it's likely stable for fields that follow a specific, exponentially decreasing form.

a binary neutron star merger in August 2017 paved the way for a new era in multimessenger astronomy. Kilonovae, produced by the expelled material from neutron star collisions, present an attractive opportunity for optical and near-infrared follow-up observations following the detection of GWs. The observation of the kilonova from GW 1780817 revealed crucial evidence for the astrophysical site of heavy element formation via the rapid neutron capture process or r-process. Given that properties of the emission are heavily influenced by the opacities of the expelled material, recent calls for enhancement in the limited available r-process atomic data have led to an increased need for precise atomic structure information. Consequently, this research aims to alleviate the present limitations in atomic structure data, focusing specifically on the Os-like isoelectronic sequence for low-charge states. Utilizing the relativistic atomic structure packages (GRASP0 and GRASP2K), the research obtained the necessary data, which included energy levels, E1, and M1 transition probabilities, along with line lists and expansion opacities for a diverse range of r-process elements. In particular, this research centered on the Os isoelectronic sequence, encompassing Os I, Ir II, Pt III, Au IV, and Hg V, with the obtained data compared to existing non-relativistic models. The research further computed the spectral energies and intensities, along with the resulting spectra of the kilonova for different wavelengths, leveraging observational data

A key factor in these neural systems is often overlooked: the quality of the acquired signals. This study assesses how noisy electrochemical signals affect the learning and generalization capabilities of a simple artificial agent and a metaheuristic algorithm inspired by nature, specifically through simulations with a silicon-based agent and a cell-like metabolic network, respectively. The investigation reveals that while both techniques can operate under harsh signal conditions, their ability to succeed and generate useful information for their environment is greatly influenced by the level of signal noise. Furthermore, this research indicates that metaheuristic methods tend to be more resilient than artificial intelligence models and heuristics in the face of noisy input signals. The findings suggest that for these types of systems to effectively learn and adapt, the quality of the acquired signals should be of a specific, moderate level of noise. This study contributes to the growing field of bio-inspired artificial intelligence and provides a foundation for exploring further developments in this field.

This study introduces a privacy-enhanced framework, referred to as TradeChain. 
This system disassociates the transaction data of participants by utilising decentralised identity systems that adhere to Self-Sovereign Identity standards. 
Key innovations in TradeChain involve the integration of distinct ledger systems: one publicly accessible, permissioned ledger for maintaining individual identities and another permissioned ledger for tracking trade activities, alongside the application of Zero Knowledge Proofs for verifying private information on trade data and allowing data owners to define customised access policies for verifying information from trade data using tokens and Ciphertext Policy Attribute-Based Encryption. 
Additionally, an experimental proof-of-concept TradeChain implementation is demonstrated on Hyperledger Indy and Fabric platforms, which shows minimal operational latency.

These powerful jets from supermassive black holes can significantly influence both the black hole's growth and its surroundings in the vast expanse of space. In the radio spectrum, these jets can be observed on various scales, but their X-ray and gamma-ray emissions are predicted to be concentrated on smaller scales, typically under 10 parsecs. Recent findings by the Chandra X-ray telescope have revealed the presence of kiloparsec-scale jets, which has sparked debate about the source of their high-energy radiation. Understanding the origins of this high-energy radiation is essential for accurately determining the physical properties and powers of these large-scale jets, which in turn affects the environment in which they reside. In this investigation, we explore the potential for the Inverse Compton interaction between relativistic electrons in jets and cosmic microwave background photons as a plausible explanation, also analyzing how this explanation could impact the observed evolution of black holes over cosmic time in jet-powered systems.

implementation of global pooling operations is often based on experience rather than a thorough theoretical understanding. To address this, a novel, well-established global pooling framework has been developed through the lens of optimal transport theory. We demonstrate that most current global pooling methods are essentially specialized solutions to an unbalanced optimal transport problem. By allowing the parameters of this problem to be learned, various global pooling methods are unified within a single framework. Consequently, a generalized global pooling layer for neural networks called UOT-Pooling (UOTP) has been proposed. To implement this UOTP layer, the classic Sinkhorn-scaling algorithm is employed. Furthermore, a new model architecture based on the Bregman ADMM algorithm is designed, which offers better numerical stability and improved ability to reproduce existing pooling layers. The proposed UOTP layers are then tested across several applications, including multi-instance learning, graph classification, and image classification, and are found to be capable of either mimicking conventional global pooling layers or developing novel, performance-enhancing pooling mechanisms.

A crucial factor contributing to this challenge may be the inherent Markovian nature of RL models, which also makes them vulnerable to deviations from this property, causing problems in modeling real-world problems. Through simulations in a practical traffic scenario, the results indicate that the proposed approach outperforms comparison methods in dynamic scenarios and enables autonomous vehicles to navigate complex urban roads.

Boost have proven effective across many fields but their high performance comes at the cost of clarity in understanding their predictions. Users are generally unable to discern how individual characteristics, or sets of characteristics, influence these models as their values change. In order to improve this understanding, a method called Disentangled Attribution Curves has been introduced to offer more transparent explanations for tree ensemble models through detailed (multi-dimensional) curves depicting feature importance at different variable values. By using this new approach, it is possible to boost the accuracy of regression models and maintain clarity in how their predictions are made, as demonstrated on real-world data and further validated in simulation studies where it was found to surpass alternative methods in recovering predictive models. Finally, a practical analysis using bike-sharing data highlights the utility of DAC in uncovering valuable new insights.

Interactions between drivers and external components like sensors and actuators pose significant challenges to embedded software development, particularly during the testing phase. Factors such as environmental unpredictability, limited hardware availability, and costs often hinder effective testing. To address these issues, this research presents a novel testing framework that targets driver verification on microcontrollers. The proposed solution involves a device under test, a duplicating counterpart, and a control unit that manages their interaction through a standardized interface. The control unit acts as a synchronous clock for their communication. A computer executes a test scenario by sending commands to the device under test and duplicating counterpart, who then respond with observed data. The testing framework can be expanded to cover multiple interfaces and various communication protocols. The validity of the proposed solution is demonstrated through successful testing of a GPIO driver.

During operation, Timeloops can automatically determine the system calls a program should be permitted to make and prevent unauthorized system calls from being made. In addition, Timeloops rectifies various shortcomings of static analysis-based techniques, such as the need for precise source code, absence of runtime threats, and the possibility of bypassing validated system calls through heap attacks. Developed using standard, publicly available tools (Bash and Stow), Timeloops is a straightforward, straightforward system call protector that does not necessitate any special hardware or additional memory to function. Our evaluation demonstrates that, on average, Timeloops is capable of stopping 78% of potentially malicious system calls while allowing benign system calls with 98% reliability. Furthermore, in a basic scenario, Timeloops is able to successfully obstruct robustness bypass techniques such as format string attacks and heap-based attacks.

The dynamic nature of social media data poses challenges to traditional approaches, including ambiguous event timelines and spaces. An innovative solution, this research introduces an adaptive spatio-temporal event detection framework leveraging social media. It addresses spatial resolution ambiguity through a quad-tree based method that segmentates regions based on data density, and uses statistical analysis incorporating the Poisson distribution to highlight anomalies in post density. Traditional adversarial training, however, tends to place an inordinate focus on predicting a specific class, thereby disregarding the uncertainty inherent in this process. Our research integrated adversarial training into a novel Bayesian framework that considers the likelihood of multiple classes and their corresponding adversarial samples. This adversarial framework is based on the premise of minimizing the distance between the Bayesian neural network's predictive distribution and a discrete, multi-class distribution known as a mixture of experts. Through empirical testing, we were able to demonstrate that our method allows for the training of BNNs on benchmark datasets that possess levels of accuracy and certainty comparable to those obtained through more conventional methods of training. Additionally, our method proves to be effective in contexts where the label data is incomplete, thereby facilitating the generation of pseudo labels through an adversarial sampling process. This pseudo labeling method is grounded in the concept of sampling from the Bayesian network's posterior distribution using adversarial samples as references. Our research demonstrates that our method allows for the reliable training of BNNs on datasets with unmarked data, outperforming existing methods in terms of both accuracy and certainty. Furthermore, our method is versatile in nature, allowing for the direct application of pseudo labeling to training data and thereby enabling the recruitment of additional human annotators on the most challenging instances. This study aimed to identify the key characteristics of effective human-human online interactions in this context, specifically focusing on service calls between English language learners and responders, which presented challenges due to the added layer of language as a potential barrier. Prior research suggested that non-native English speakers faced more significant obstacles in effective online interactions. To address this, the study analyzed service calls to determine whether language status (native or non-native) influenced success in online interactions, measured by call completion time and members' overall satisfaction. Data from a large call center involving over 450k calls were manually reviewed by trained staff to assess the quality of over 272k calls. Statistical models revealed that calls involving English language learners tended to last about 2 minutes longer and had lower quality scores compared to native English speaker calls. Nevertheless, both language groups exhibited similar percentages of successful calls. Notably, other factors, such as agent performance, also significantly predicted call quality, while language status played a relatively minor role. Furthermore, despite initial concerns, language differences did not hinder online interactions according to multiple success indicators. Ultimately, the findings suggest that service calls involving English language learners can be effective and satisfying for all parties involved.

focus on adversarial robustness, a critical consideration in RL that deals with the challenge of learning a nearly optimal policy when a fraction of data in the training set has been compromised by an adversary. Our study begins by examining a worst-case scenario involving the linear reinforcement learning problem and demonstrating that even in this scenario, the optimal policy can be learned using data with a purity of at least O(1/lnT) when the reward is bounded. This result is significant as it matches the best known threshold prior to our research and remains relatively high even in the presence of adversarial interference. Furthermore, we have expanded our findings to include both linear and general RL models featuring a finite number of features and adversarial contamination affecting at least an O(1/lnT) fraction of data in the training set. In each case, we have developed algorithms to compute a nearly optimal policy with a relative error of at most O(lnT) compared to the optimal policy. These algorithms utilize standard robust loss functions and remain relatively simple to execute. Our research also involves theoretical analysis involving threat models that involve adversarial rewards in the data and is therefore of interest to the RL and ML communities.

We introduce a kernel-based approach to generating data-driven models for high-dimensional, nonlinear systems. a specific type of matter collapse, governed by a certain relationship between pressure and density, behaves according to the general theory of relativity. The effect of this relationship on the mass function is analyzed in terms of its consistency with the general relativity equations, and we find that when this relationship holds, it's usually difficult to get consistent solutions. The outcomes of this type of collapse are then explored, along with the effect of additional factors, such as pressure in a collapsing cloud. Since accurately modeling such a situation is hard due to lack of information about its dynamics, we consider small changes in density instead. These small changes cause tiny pressures and allow us to analyze the behavior numerically. Our study reveals that when there is pressure in a collapsing cloud, the equilibrium radius initially increases with increasing mass, in contrast to what is expected from the Einstein fluid model where smaller objects are always more compact than larger ones. Later stages of collapse follow a pattern similar to that predicted by the Einstein fluid model, with smaller objects experiencing greater levels of compression.

we have developed a comprehensive method for determining corrections to the extremality bounds and entropy of Kerr-Newman black holes following any arbitrary perturbation. This method involves integrating an effective stress tensor and shows, under certain conditions, the correction is equivalent to the standard stress tensor, thereby illuminating the relationship between extremality corrections and energy conditions. Furthermore, we have demonstrated that to lower the mass of an extremal black hole in a canonical ensemble as stipulated by the weak gravity conjecture, the perturbation must breach the dominant energy condition. We have successfully applied this method to compute higher-order corrections to black holes in anti-de Sitter space and to Kerr black holes.

fracture instability have been achieved for 2D dynamic fracture. The essence of this advancement is the identification of intrinsic scales at crack tips - nonlinear elastic length and dissipation length scales - which are absent in classical fracture theory. Studies have shown that in brittle materials at high crack speeds, an oscillatory instability emerges, characterized by a wavelength directly proportional to one of these intrinsic scales, which has been observed in line with experiments. Through phase-field fracture models, we find the following features of this oscillatory instability: (i) It also exists in materials with linear elastic behavior near the crack, depending solely on dissipation properties; (ii) It undergoes a type of supercritical bifurcation; and (iii) It's minimally affected by factors like the fracture energy associated with a certain dissipation time. These results support the idea that this oscillatory instability is an inherent feature of fast cracks in 2D, while we also show that an ultra-high speed instability can be attributed to a limiting rate of energy transport near the crack. The numerical framework of the fracture approach used in this study is thoroughly described.

AI is increasingly becoming essential for handling the unpredictability of black-box machine learning methods, particularly in healthcare and data protection regulations. However, standard visualizations often fall short due to their inability to differentiate between subtle feature variations, which can significantly affect a model's outcome. This paper addresses these limitations by introducing an integrated solution that combines visual and numerical aspects of feature importance through a correlation-based weighted scatter plot, complete with confidence intervals that facilitate actionable decision-making. The proposed solution, which can be applied to various methods for assigning feature importance, offers a clear and comprehensive understanding of how features contribute to a model's prediction.

graphene holds significant promise, enabling the synthesis of highly lattice-mismatched materials and reducing waste from expensive substrate reuse. Nevertheless, concrete proof of a remote epitaxial process is yet to be found. Many instances are instead attributed to contaminants between graphene and the substrate, such as Ru or Cu, or alternative processes including van der Waals epitaxy or a solvation process. This study discovered that when growing the Heusler compound GdPtSb on clean graphene substrates, it results in a random alloy instead of epitaxy. However, testing with a range of transition metal dopants on graphene revealed that only those in group 4 [Ti, Zr, Hf] and 5 [V, Cr, Mn] exhibit a remote epitaxial process on a Ru substrate. The epitaxial interface is shown to be superior to a random alloy, as evidenced by better crystal alignment, electronic properties, and catalytic performance for water splitting. The remote epitaxial process has potential to expand the scope of high-lattice-mismatch heteroepitaxy using monolayer graphene as a substrate.

A new method allows us to make this analysis without knowing whether certain assumptions hold or even what values some important statistics have. By using information about the matrix of average relationships among these time series, we create an estimator of how many common random patterns there are, even in cases with extreme data fluctuations. As sample size increases, the rates of divergence for the matrix's key properties are significantly faster than others. To improve estimation rate, we use this information to create a simplified method. A related test is also developed to verify whether the assumptions hold. A demonstration of the effectiveness of our estimators in practice is given through a simulation using data from thousands of individual human genomes. By using this data without sharing the actual data, we estimate that there are approximately 329,000 common random patterns in human DNA.

For a given hyperbolic surface that a pair of measured foliations, denoted by $\mathsf{F}_{+}$ and $\mathsf{F}_{-}$, completely fill, our analysis reveals that when sufficiently small, multiplying both $\mathsf{F}_{+}$ and $\mathsf{F}_{-}$ by a factor of $t>0$ results in unique representations as the foliations measured at infinity for a corresponding quasi-Fuchsian three-dimensional manifold. This new manifold is essentially an extended version of the given surface that approaches an infinite real number. Our finding is similar to another known theorem which asserts that a nearly Fuchsian three-dimensional manifold is uniquely defined based on certain laminations measured along the boundary of its convex core. Our results can also be applied to understand half-pipe geometry. Our work extends previous findings by M. Braun which focused on quasi-Fuchsian groups that contain a specific torsion element. Developing effective Question Answering (Q&A) systems capable of addressing this issue has been a challenging task, especially considering the lack of labeled data. Unlike other information extraction tasks, labeling QAs involves task-specific challenges such as coordinating answers across multiple sections of a paper, making existing labeling approaches unsuitable. These studies revealed neutrino instabilities within the context of the former explosion, specifically within a 1-3 millisecond time frame and in specific regions such as the neutrino oscillation driver and its surrounding area, as well as within a 0.1-0.5 millimeter radius radius of the neutrino-sourced material's boundary. Unfortunately, existing solutions have failed to present a unified, comprehensive approach applicable to different domains and available for public access. In response, our project offers the first publicly accessible, web-based acronym identification and disambiguation platform capable of processing acronyms in scientific, biomedical, and general domains. This system can be accessed via the website http://iq.cs.uoregon.edu:5000 and supplemented with a demo video available at https://youtu.be/IkSh7LqI42M. Furthermore, the system's source code has been made available for further exploration at https://github.com/amirveyseh/MadDog.

, is one of the most notable manifestations of quantum physics. Historically, quantum interference has been observed in charge transport; however, recent findings indicate that it also significantly affects thermal properties. This insight enables the precise manipulation of heat within microscopic devices through phase-coherence. This study showcases how exploiting phase-coherent edge states in quantum Hall systems allows for the realization of exceptional thermoelectric properties and efficient heat rectification. A multi-quantum point contact tunneling setup with multiple interference paths was used to demonstrate that these systems break electron-hole symmetry. As a result, an electron charge current can be directed from hot to cold or vice versa, and an accompanying heat current is also predicted. These findings can be attributed to a simple and logical physical interpretation. Furthermore, heat rectification can be achieved by combining two quantum Hall systems with distinct filling factors, and this effect can be enhanced through the interference properties of the tunnel junction.

Although one-dimensional topological structures are widely understood, the concept of 1D topological orders is still a subject of debate. This research utilizes advanced analytical tools to explore the determinants of wave velocity in two distinct systems: one governed by the FitzHugh-Nagumo equations and another modeled by the Oregonator equations. and Wilson algorithms create random spanning trees through random walks, and this research examines their synergy with the aim of reducing tree construction time. Demonstrating statistical equivalence on particular stopping points by analyzing 'branches' produced by these algorithms on random graphs reveals that these algorithms can generate the same trees by employing a 'time reversal' technique. This statistical equivalence enables a faster method to determine whether two random spanning trees are identical by utilizing this branch splitting strategy. Furthermore, this research provides a novel method for estimating the cover time of random walks, which has implications for determining the time complexity of the Wilson's algorithm modification. In particular, this research shows that this modification is linear on trees and hypergrees of bounded degree, and it offers a new technique for studying the evolution of random graphs, such as the random regular graph of bounded degree. In contrast, the random graph model $G(n,m)$ proves to be less suitable for studying the Wilson's algorithm on this model as the algorithm doesn't have a meaningful stopping point, and thus, no equivalent relationship can be established.

SARS-CoV-2 in 2020, was officially classified as a global health crisis by the WHO. As a result, the world is relying heavily on public health precautions such as social distancing measures to curb the virus spread and maintain the healthcare system functionality. With the isolation of communities, access to reliable information has become restricted. Consequently, the health minister in South Africa updates the public every day on COVID-19 infections, including affected individuals' demographic details. This ministry employs various methods to disseminate this information widely. As part of the national effort to mitigate the pandemic, a mobile application was developed to provide verified information to users in South Africa. Utilizing NLP techniques, the app categorizes input user queries and retrieves relevant information from a pre-loaded database to respond accordingly. Additionally, the app adheres to data protection principles by encrypting user data and protecting their anonymity. Following successful deployment, the application demonstrated its capability to efficiently disseminate information to users across the country. Notably, our data analysis revealed that the majority of users reside in major cities, and their inquiry patterns indicate a focus on understanding infection dynamics in individuals and overall infection statistics. This study was conducted as part of a national project to issue regular daily reports on COVID-19 infections in South Africa.

During training, we discovered that the relationship proposal distribution is skewed, with the majority of incorrect relationships being easily identified due to poor object detection. As a result, low-frequency difficult proposals struggle to contribute effectively. Our proposed framework, Spatially-Aware Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (SABRA), mitigates the impact of false positives in VRD tasks. To counter the imbalance, SABRA incorporates Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (BNPS), which divides proposals into distinct sub-classes based on difficulty and samples a balanced distribution accordingly. By employing this strategy, BNPS yields an optimized model performance and a notable decrease in false positives. To address low-frequency difficult proposals, we designed a spatially-aware sampling mechanism that prioritizes them and ensures a shared learning experience among them. In addition to improving model performance, SABRA is versatile and can be applied to a variety of proposal sampling methods. Our approach successfully addresses the source of high false positives in VRD and achieves state-of-the-art results on the COCO-Instance37 and COCO-Instance90 datasets.

Large Hadron Collider (LHC) will discover new physics. However, the energy level of the LHC may not be sufficient to determine the nature of this new physics. Therefore, it is likely that a first sign of this new physics will be discovered at a future high-energy collider, such as the Future Circular Collider (FCC), which would serve as a follow-up project. In this research, we investigate how the new physics signal can be reconstructed at the FCC using information gathered from LHC experiments. Our study focuses on three distinct forms of new physics: supersymmetric partners, universal extra dimensions, and a scalar singlet. For each of these scenarios, we develop reconstruction methods that take into account the fidelity of the FCC in detecting particles and the uncertainty of the LHC measurement. Ultimately, we evaluate the capabilities of the FCC in reconstructing these new physics models.

Hawking radiation from primordial black holes could be the source behind the observed excess radiowave signals. By assuming that dark matter exists entirely as these black holes, we calculated that the temperature resulting from Hawking radiation is negligible in comparison to the cosmic microwave background, primarily due to the black holes' low mass. This is caused by the emission's power law suppression of lower-energy frequencies. Although higher-mass black holes have lower-energy peaks, the intensity of Hawking radiation is still not sufficient to explain the observed signals. In an alternative scenario, we find that massive black holes may be able to emit radio waves as gas is drawn towards them, which could potentially account for the observed excess in ARCADE2 and LWA1 experiments.

rotation pattern within a less massive and less luminous star that has evolved into a giant. Typically, lower and intermediate mass stars retain their rapid rotation rates during their main sequence phase. However, once these stars expand into giants, we expect a faster core rotation rate compared to their outer layers. Contrary to these expectations, KIC 9267654's rotation speed is observed to be higher near its surface rather than at its core, which presents a challenge to angular momentum conservation principles. To validate our findings, we updated the constraints based on spectroscopic surface measurements, verified that the detected oscillation patterns align with the previously determined core and outer layer rotation rates, and confirmed that the star exhibits no significant chemical abnormalities. Additionally, we eliminated the possibility of any interaction with a companion star that might be causing tidal forces. Lastly, we examined possible explanations for this unusual internal rotation profile, including the possibility of the star ingesting a giant planet or experiencing enhanced angular momentum redistribution through tidal inertial waves induced by a nearby substellar companion.

Despite being widely adopted, the RAM model lacks a solid theoretical foundation, characterized by inconsistent definitions and a lack of cohesive results. This research aims to rectify this issue by presenting a new RAM model with desirable algorithmic properties and robust complexity classes, particularly linear-time computability for problems like LIN and CONST-DELAY-lin, an enumeration class of problems that can be computed after linear-time preprocessing. The proposed computation model has limited storage and processing capabilities - its registers can store $O(N)$ elements, where $N$ is the input size, and operations take unit time. The success of this foundation will be built upon demonstrating that a RAM with only basic addition operations can perform essential arithmetic operations efficiently after initial linear-time processing. Additionally, despite the large register size, the model will not support operations exceeding linear time for input size $N$.

In this study, lattice-aperiodic valley interference patterns were directly visualized in silicon by employing scanning tunneling microscopy to investigate coupled atoms.

A robust weather detection system is crucial for seamless operation of transportation services in diverse weather conditions.

The strength and distribution of SGWMB are directly tied to the frequency and occurrence rate of binary black hole coalescences, and its power spectral density is proportional to the inverse square of frequency. Unlike the more common gravitational wave background produced by binary black holes, SGWMB's characteristics allow it to span a broader frequency range due to the Brownian motion behavior, and therefore dominates at higher frequencies. Failing to accurately account for SGWMB could lead to incorrect conclusions, but properly investigating it might provide insight into the detection strategies of gravitational waves. Furthermore, studying SGWMB offers a novel method to pinpoint the location of binary black hole events.

A primary factor driving this attention lies in the word prediction challenge, where given a sequence of words in a sentence, a model is tasked with recommending the subsequent word. Researchers have addressed this issue through various techniques, combining either syntactic or semantic analysis methods in the past. However, individually, these approaches often fail to yield practical results in real-world applications. A hybrid word suggestion model proposed here, combining the strengths of Naive Bayes and latent semantic analysis and considering context provided by surrounding words in the sentence, demonstrates considerable promise. Traditionally, this relies on having access to the original network's training data and parameters, which isn't always feasible due to storage or privacy constraints in real-world applications. This study introduces decision-based black-box knowledge distillation, allowing a model to be trained on the behavior of a network whose internal workings are inaccessible, as long as it produces classification outputs. When access to the original data is possible, a training sample's resistance to other classes is quantified by measuring the distance between its class and the network's decision boundaries, which is used to assign a soft label to the sample. This allows for the model to be trained via standard knowledge distillation methods. When access to the original data isn't possible, pseudo-samples are created based on the network's decision boundaries and assigned soft labels, which serve as a transfer set for training the model. Our proposed approach is evaluated on multiple networks and datasets and shows positive results. Code is available at: https://github.com/zwang84/zsdb3kd.

In this research, we introduce a pioneering Co-Imitation Learning framework to circumvent this issue. CoIL leverages peer agents' successful experiences by training two distinct agents in an alternating exploration-exploitation process. Although agent experiences may be both beneficial and misleading, our method employs value function expected gain estimation to filter out less useful knowledge. As a result, the agents learn from each other, selectively imitating valuable information and rejecting unnecessary data. the growth of data-driven modeling in mechanics, making cooperative modeling more feasible. As research advances, diverse teams can create new models and data, leading to shared knowledge and collaboration opportunities. Nevertheless, a challenge persists in neural networks' tendency to 'forget' previous tasks after training on new ones. This drawback restricts cooperative learning, since adjusting an existing model to address a new problem can negatively affect performance on earlier tasks handled by other teams. To address this issue, the authors developed a groundbreaking 'continual learning' method and successfully implemented it in solid mechanics for the first time. They utilized recurrent neural networks to predict the behavior of materials undergoing plasticity. Notably, the developed method can be adapted for use in a wide range of network architectures and to predict multiple phenomena. This study's purpose is to stimulate innovative applications of continual learning, facilitating collaborative strategies among the mechanics community in addressing increasingly complex problems. Results demonstrate that the employed method can enable sequential learning of multiple constitutive laws without memory loss and often with reduced data requirements, matching or exceeding the accuracy achieved through standard training of separate models for each law.

-density parity-check (LDPC) codes usually assume the independence of degree distributions from edge endpoints. In contrast, our research extends this understanding by investigating LDPC ensembles that incorporate degree-degree correlations. We propose novel techniques for generating degree-degree correlated LDPC ensembles, derive density evolution equations applicable to binary erasure channels, and employ numerical simulations to illustrate how degree-degree correlations impact LDPC code performance. Interestingly, our findings indicate that negative degree-degree correlations can enhance the maximum error tolerance of LDPC codes, with further increases potentially yielding superior unequal error protection designs.

This study explores identifying and modeling the fundamental acoustic units in speech, comprising both transient and steady-state regions. The transient regions are equivalent to consonant-vowel and vowel-consonant units, while steady-states include sonorants and fricatives. The speech signal is first segmented into CVC-like units based on a short-term energy contour and then grouped using graph clustering, where the earliness of transitions between units determines branching in the graph. The resulting acoustic units are initially represented as hidden markov models and then optimized using vector quantization. An apec-based synthesis system is then developed to successfully produce speech without transcription. Our experiments demonstrate that the proposed system is capable of delivering comparable performance to existing methods, particularly in cases where the target language's phoneme inventory is very different from that of English.

manipulation of quantum states using probabilistic protocols constrained by specific quantum resource limitations.
Initially, we formulated a fundamental criterion for achieving a physical transformation between quantum states using a previously introduced resource metric.
This approach led to the discovery that the metric is not only necessary, but also sufficient, for one-sided extraction of maximum entropy from quantum states of a particular form, thereby refining previous research in this area.
Building upon this finding, we adapted the method to investigate the most efficient probabilistic protocols for converting quantum states into target states with limited quantum resources.
A distinct approach employed a linear programming model to determine the maximum achievement of desired transformations from a set of initial quantum states under resource constraints.
This method enabled us to identify the most efficient mixed probabilistic protocols for converting quantum states into target states with limited quantum resources.

the process by which massive star formation occurs under the influence of strong nearby magnetism is studied. The development of cloud structure and fragmentation is closely tied to how magnetic forces are balanced against gravitational pulls. Although fluctuations in density and magnetic field strength are common, they have distinct effects on the probability of massive star creation. An investigation of the role of magnetic energy in the cloud's overall structure reveals that too little magnetic energy leads to fragmentation and formation of massive stars, but in contrast, strong magnetic forces can stall the transformation of fragmenting structures into massive objects. A critical threshold for magnetic energy within the cloud is identified, below which magnetic forces can't halt fragmentation. By examining magnetic energy at this critical threshold and total cloud mass, the range in massive star formation efficiency can be explained. The formation of massive stars is influenced by magnetic forces in two opposing ways, a dominant effect when magnetic energy is low and an opposing effect when magnetic energy near the threshold maximization is high.

The conventional method for describing optical properties uses a velocity-based approach tied to the vector potential. An alternative method exists, where a finite system is represented through the electric field, resulting in a dipole-based model inspired by Peierls substitution. This study evaluates the accuracy of both methods in relation to gauge invariance, utilizing TB models constructed from maximally localized Wannier functions and applied to two-dimensional paradigm materials. Our investigation shows that the velocity-based method is precise within the context of a finite system, and when extended to infinite systems, it adheres to the minimal coupled Maxwell-Tight Binding (MCTB) model despite potential discrepancies. The dipole-based model is found to be equivalent to the velocity-based method when expressed in a gauge-invariant basis derived from Peierls substitution. We identify a novel approach, known as MCTB-reduction, for converting any tight-binding model into a dipole-based form that is gauge-invariant and valid for both finite and infinite systems. MCTB-reduction provides a strategy to incorporate quantum effects from tight-binding models into dipole-based models that fail gauge invariance.

known as the all-versus-nothing proof is presented without the use of inequalities. This concept consists of two main species, referred to as "always-type" and "sometimes-type", which have received significant research attention. Past studies on "always-type" all-versus-nothing proofs have primarily involved perfect correlations from stabilizer states. This has led many researchers to conclude that perfect correlations are the sole means of yielding "always-type" all-versus-nothing proofs. Contrary to this prevailing notion, our study offers a "always-type" all-versus-nothing proof rooted in non-perfect correlations. This research aims to clarify an enduring misconception and potentially expands our understanding of Bell nonlocality while also opening avenues for advancements in quantum information theory.

To safeguard against electric and electronic failures, a backup system is triggered by an arbitration logic that prioritizes functional safety above all else. To uphold the standards set forth by ISO 26262, rigorous testing of this logic is mandatory. Through this validation, one can confidently ensure the reliability of system responses in times of crisis and prevent aberrant system states from materializing. Traditional verification tools often fall short in this regard, prompting us to investigate an alternative solution based on formal methods. Specifically, we focus on utilizing predicate transformation to identify and test system failures from a high-level perspective, thus embodying the spirit of functional safety. By leveraging this approach, we are able to validate a high-level failure detection architecture built around fault isolation, fault protection, and safety monitoring, thereby validating its conformance to safety requirements. Furthermore, we demonstrate the application of this methodology to a real-world parking assistant system, leveraging composition and predicate transformation to prove system-wide failure detection, and identifying key failures that need to be detected to prevent system states harmful to safety. By employing SMT solvers to verify failure detection capabilities from a high-level perspective, we are able to validate a system that meets the requirements set forth in safety Level 2, thereby providing an alternative solution that is more suitable for system-level verification when compared to local verification.

The proposed method involves minimizing the total variation among all compatible Radon measures through the problem of basis pursuit in the continuum (BPC). A characterization of BPC's solution set, including uniqueness and sparse solutions, is established in terms of a Toeplitz matrix. The uniqueness and characteristics of BPC's solution rely on the eigenvalue properties of this matrix. The solutions range from a single, weighted Dirac mass for certain conditions to infinitely many Dirac masses in other cases. The number of Dirac masses in each case is influenced by the rank of a positive or negative semi-definite matrix. The positive or negative definiteness of the matrix also determines the weights of the Dirac masses as either nonnegative or nonpositive, respectively. aviart-Thomas elements are widely used to approximate vector-valued variables like velocity or momentum. Nevertheless, the standard finite element methods that employ the lowest-order quadrilateral Raviart-Thomas elements tend to have low spatial accuracy in the vector transport problem. This issue arises because the low-order Raviart-Thomas elements have only one degree of freedom per element that contributes to the vector gradient, resulting in a non-conservative discretization that complicates the solution of the associated scalar transport problem. This, in turn, can lead to instabilities and even numerical convergence issues, especially when the transport is combined with free surfaces and interface capture issues. To resolve these problems, we have developed a new method based on the hybridizable finite element method (HFEM) that specifically addresses the vector transport problem. This method leverages the hybridizable nature of the rotationally invariant VEM-RT elements to eliminate intermediate variables and streamline the discretization, thereby enhancing the space-time accuracy of the solution. Compared to the conventional finite element method, the HFEM method offers several benefits, including better space-time accuracy, the ability to solve weakly nonlinear problems, and efficient large-scale simulations on multiple GPUs without the need for complex adaptivity. We have validated our new method by applying it to a variety of numerical experiments, including interface capture, free surfaces, and mass conservation in the transport problem. These experiments have shown that the HFEM method is an effective and efficient method for solving the vector transport problem.

To address these problems, experts employ fairness metrics, decentralized machine learning methods, and differential privacy models, often within static data settings. In contrast, learning processes that occur over time, particularly those using sequential models, have been overlooked. This work addresses a pressing issue where temporal deep learning models are used to analyze time-stamped data, yet their designs often disregard the inherent nature of temporal sequences and the resulting dependencies between data points. These limitations lead to significant concerns about the fairness of predictions made by these models and the sensitivity of their predictions when dealing with confidential information. To tackle these challenges, novel concepts of temporal fairness and sensitivity are introduced, along with the development of corresponding metrics. A decentralized learning approach centered on fairness and sensitivity is proposed, alleviating the shortcomings of existing models that have prioritized either aspect exclusively. This method leverages the principles of Markov chains and decentralized machine learning to create a dynamic framework, the fairness and sensitivity characteristics of which are rigorously analyzed and demonstrated through concrete implementations.

The incorporation of artificial intelligence (AI) into this task has improved it, allowing high-quality classifiers to detect attacks efficiently; however, these classifiers demand substantial computing power or memory. The scenario presents a problem, particularly when these classifiers need to operate on low-resource devices or prevent performance overload on devices with IoT or industrial applications. A novel solution to overcome this challenge is proposed by NBcoded, a light attack classification tool that effectively combines noisy data removal and efficient data encoding, leveraging the benefits of Naive Bayes classifier while reducing resource requirements. In this study, three NBcoded implementations are developed using three Naive Bayes likelihood distribution assumptions (Gaussian, Complement, and Bernoulli). By comparing the results, NBcoded's performances are evaluated on well-known intrusion detection datasets, with a special focus on removing noisy data from datasets, and the outcomes reveal that NBcoded outperforms traditional machine learning classifiers in several cases, including a substantial 75% reduction in processing time with Complement Naive Bayes implementation.

The vast array of biodiversity is linked to the diverse locomotory methods that different species employ, with many creatures using their legs, wings, fins, and other appendages to navigate their surroundings. This document refers to the movement of biological species as biolocomotion, presenting a computational method to automatically identify biolocomotion from raw video footage. Scaling the distances of a space by a positive factor yields a transformed metric space, belonging to the same Gromov--Hausdorff class. This type of transformation can cause some clouds to jump into others, as noted in our previous study. To explain this phenomenon, we investigated the stability of these space transformations. This paper demonstrates that any cloud having a stabilizer with nontrivial action will contain a unique central metric space, such that transformations from the stabilizer all converge to this space, thereby indicating that it is zero distance away from all others within that group. The key proof for this lies within our previously established cloud completeness theorem.

Building on this principle, our research explores how digital-analog simulation can be used to study fermionic systems, specifically the Fermi-Hubbard model, by mapping it into an equivalent fermionic Hamiltonian with interactive qubits. Focusing on the effects of qubit connectivity, tunneling magnitude, and system size, particularly for a 1D and 2D fermionic system with nearest-neighbor interactions, our findings indicate that these fermionic systems exhibit accurate simulation when the connectivity matches the interaction pattern for a given system size. Additionally, our research includes the simulation of a 2D Hubbard model with a range beyond nearest-neighbor interactions, showing that the level of complexity increases with the range of interactions and the number of non-nearest-neighbor qubits. Given the current technological constraints of quantum computing, our strategy of minimizing the number of measurements required to study these fermionic systems could offer significant advantages. Furthermore, our research includes the implementation details of these simulations using the analog simulation capabilities of the IBM Quantum Experience, illustrating the trade-offs that arise from the differences between the capabilities of the hardware and the requirements of the systems being studied.

To address these challenges, we've developed a novel weighted-mutation-assisted genetic algorithm (WMA-GA) with an R-squared-based fitness function that enhances image clarity, precision, and rapid convergence in forming complex structures within scattering media. As a companion technology to our binary WMA-GA system, we've designed a swift, economical, and reliable iterative wavefront manipulation system that utilizes an affordable ferroelectric liquid crystal (FLC)-based binary-phase spatial light modulator (SLM). This wavefront manipulation system enables the creation of numerous complex 3D patterns and rapid concentration of light within or through scattering media. To evaluate our approach, we've demonstrated the realization of multiple complex 3D patterns, such as Lady of Mang Yuan, Peacock, and Tibetan Tiger, as well as rapid focus switching between 10 cm and 20 cm in a scattering medium using our proposed technique. To the best of our knowledge, our approach demonstrates the first practical application of genetic algorithms in focusing light through scattering mediums.

Due to the need for smaller time steps for resolving particle collisions, traditional models can become computationally expensive for large-scale simulations involving numerous particles. Existing methods often involve artificially lengthening collision time steps to several times the time steps used in flow simulations, however this can lead to biased simulation results. Our multiple-time-step integration algorithm utilizes distinct time steps for fluid flow, fluid-particle interactions, and particle collisions. This method successfully eliminates the bias caused by varying time steps by modeling collision processes at a much finer resolution within a slightly longer time frame. Our simulation results show that this algorithm produces accurate solutions and matches simulations using traditional methods. Furthermore, we found that our method is resistant to errors in both conservative mass and overall balance when simulating particle collisions.

the Unruh/Hawking process of black holes and the heat radiation of cosmological black holes has led to a universal principle in quantum field theory: the divergence of the momentum flux near the horizon inevitably results in the continuation of radiation. This study demonstrates that such divergence is a fundamental characteristic of the flux leakage through the event horizon. As a result, the energy spectrum of the radiation emitted in the Unruh/Hawking process and cosmic radiation cannot be explained by the low-frequency mode of the Klein-Gordon field near the static potential well or the decay of the coherent states, respectively. As the number of emitted quanta increases without bounds, the energy spectrum of the radiation is inevitably powered by negative energy states. The primary physical mechanism driving the radiation in both situations is the process of non-perturbative tunneling involving leakage and negative energy states. This mechanism is capable of offering an innovative understanding of the cosmic radiation phenomenon.

Nevertheless, the volatility of system caches still poses a challenge, as data in these caches may be lost in the event of a crash, necessitating an explicit flush into the main memory to guarantee data integrity. In this study, a new algorithm-based approach is proposed to guarantee data consistency and correctness for high-performance computing applications in systems using non-volatile memory. This method introduces only a minor runtime overhead, allowing developers to leverage the properties of algorithms to verify data integrity after system crashes. Our proposed approach demonstrates significant advantages over traditional checkpointing methods in terms of runtime efficiency while maintaining the ability to correct errors with minimal reprocessing costs. Our comprehensive evaluations, carried out across multiple test scenarios and algorithms such as an iterative solver and dense matrix multiplication, have consistently yielded a remarkably low overhead, at most 8.2 percent in some instances, with most experiments averaging under 3 percent, thereby making this approach an attractive solution for ensuring fault-tolerant HPC applications.

Our work also includes a numerical model that illustrates the extreme fluctuations in the dissipation range of turbulence at an instant in time, as well as its averaging properties over both time and space. This model reveals the onset of strongly non-Gaussian behavior in the velocity differences at the Kolmogorov microscale during short periods of time, with a skewness of approximately $-20$ in natural units. We delve into the concept of redundancy among association rules from a theoretical perspective. Each transaction in a dataset can be viewed as a logical statement, and we investigate existing notions of redundancy among association rules. We explore alternative definitions of redundancy and introduce new characterizations, highlighting relationships between these concepts. We demonstrate that two distinct notions of redundancy exist, differing in how full-confidence implications are treated. We establish a deduction calculus for each of these concepts, show how to create the smallest possible bases, and also examine redundancy with multiple association rules. Building upon expander graphs, high dimensional expanders play a vital role in theoretical computer science but unfortunately, there are only a few constructions available that offer arbitrarily small local spectral expansion.

Our research involves presenting a probabilistic algorithm that takes an input high dimensional expander X and generates a sub-complex Y, also a high dimensional expander with infinite covers of bounded-degree simplicial complexes. The generated Y preserves X's graph structure, reducing link complexity and inherits a sparsified form of X's links when the link size of X is O(log |X|). The basis of this algorithm is rooted in Lubotzky, Samuels, and Vishne's groups from 2005 that created the first discovered high dimensional expanders.

Incorporating our methods also reveals a novel sparsification algorithm for high dimensional expanders, maintaining its key local spectral characteristics, offering an area of independent interest.

The problem of pinpointing which training examples are responsible for a trained model's inaccuracies or biases has gained significant attention over the past decade. The computation of the Shapley value for training examples with respect to validation accuracy and model fairness has become a popular framework for tackling this issue. Although recent studies have made progress in computing the Shapley value for a single machine learning model in isolation, they fail to account for a comprehensive machine learning pipeline consisting of data preprocessing, feature extraction, and model training. To bridge this gap, a new system, DataScope, has been designed to efficiently compute the Shapley value for training examples within an end-to-end machine learning pipeline using a self-supervised learning approach. DataScope's novel scheme leverages self-supervised learning to dynamically create a series of proxy models that can explain the model's behavior across preprocessing, feature extraction, and model training. By combining these proxy models with minimax optimization, DataScope can quickly compute the Shapley value even for large training sets containing thousands of examples. The system's effectiveness has been verified through experiments involving several datasets, including ImageNet, and has been successfully applied to identify problematic training examples causing the model's unfairness on group-level features.

Theoretical models predict that when exposed to pressure, Mn$_3$Sn undergoes a significant transformation, where the distances between certain atoms in the material change significantly, stabilizing a helical magnetic ground state. Experiments have demonstrated that at pressures exceeding 1.5 GPa, the material's anomalous Hall effect is entirely eliminated. The pressure-dependent magnetization study revealed that as pressure increased, Mn$_3$Sn shifted from a conventional antiferromagnetic ground state to a helical state, where a required characteristic for the anomalous Hall effect is absent. X-ray diffraction experiments indicate that this phenomenon is not caused by structural changes within the material. The investigation further reveals that when Mn$_3$Sn enters the helical state, its in-plane lattice parameter exhibits unusual temperature dependence, where the material's parameter $c/a$ ratios increase. This discovery is consistent with theoretical predictions, where Mn$_3$Sn's helical ground state is predicted to exhibit unusual temperature dependence. Ultimately, this study significantly contributes to understanding the material's anomalous Hall effect, as well as its structural and magnetic properties under high pressure conditions.
