Our framework accounts for the movement of Population III binary remnants during the formation of the universe's structure and identifies which of these remnants fall into nuclear star clusters through gravitational interaction with field stars. Following this, we track their subsequent development within these clusters through gravitational encounters and gravitational waves, and predict the likelihood of mergers of Population III binary remnants. Our study shows that about 7.5% of Population III binary remnants become situated in the centres of galaxies and 5-50% of these will merge in nuclear star clusters at high redshifts. These events peak at z=5-7 with a merger rate of 0.4-10 years^-1 Gpc^-3. Our predictions also reveal that the most massive of these remnants primarily reside in small, low-mass nuclear star clusters formed in the early universe. These clusters host black holes of masses 40-85 M_\\odot that can produce detections similar to GW190521, specifically in a mass range typically found for this detected merger. Our results indicate that detections like GW190521 may originate from a combination of both mergers of Population III binary remnants and standard mergers of binary black hole systems formed from star clusters.

Research using precision medicine approaches and computational tools has shown that even recently approved SARS-CoV-2 antigens may not provide sufficient protection against this variant. Therefore, there is an urgent need for an efficient method to update existing vaccines to account for emerging viruses. By combining computational analysis of immune responses with existing vaccine formulations, researchers can assess the effectiveness of updating vaccines using different strategies. In this study, researchers focused on developing an innovative type of vaccine called vector vaccines, specifically those based on Ad26 and Ad13 vectors. By incorporating multiple BA.5 fragments into these vectors, researchers found that including three fragments led to the best immune response, closely matching that triggered by SARS-CoV-2 infection. Notably, even a single dose of these updated vectors triggered protective antibody levels 14 days after injection. Another effective approach involved combining existing COVID-19 vaccines with BA.5 fragments, using a low dose resulted in a strong immune response comparable to that triggered by SARS-CoV-2 infection. By applying computational tools to real-world data, researchers found that including BA.5 fragments into Ad26 and Ad13 vaccine candidates for booster shots would significantly enhance protection against this variant, with potential benefits extending to other SARS-like viruses.

Neural Networks (DCNNs), are capable of generating robust image representations, but are limited when dealing with orientation transformations. To address this limitation, we have developed a novel model called Orientation Convolutional Neural Networks (OCNNs) that can handle transformations up to 90 degrees. Our OCNN framework is an extension of traditional DCNNs, where two separate branches process images from different axes, and by combining them, we can handle orientations up to 90 degrees. Additionally, we have introduced a method for fusing the axes and developed a method for evaluating orientation-dependent performance metrics. Our findings show that OCNNs outperform existing methods in dealing with orientations and perform similarly when dealing with transformations of less than 90 degrees. Our unique evaluation approach provides valuable insights into the performance of orientation-dependent models. Finally, we have successfully applied our OCNN framework to the task of plane detection and achieved impressive results, setting a new benchmark in the process.

graph convolutional networks (GCNs) in point cloud learning. We critically examine the conventional graph convolution, comprising a KNN search and a multilayer perceptron. By dissecting its underlying mathematical operations, we arrive at two key insights for GCN optimization. Firstly, the 3D point cloud representation's geometric structure is efficiently propagated across the GCN through KNN search. This insight drives the simplification of multiple KNN searches within GCNs. Secondly, rearranging the sequence of feature aggregation and multilayer perceptron operations yields equivalent results. Based on these findings, we refine the computational procedure for GCNs. Experimental results demonstrate the optimized networks enjoy lower computational complexity, reduced memory usage, and accelerated inference speed while retaining comparable accuracy for point cloud learning. The source code will be publicly available at the GitHub repository: https://github.com/ofsoundof/EfficientGCN.git.

New studies emphasize the significance of considering volatile depletion in star composition to predict the bulk composition and internal structures of these planets. In this research, we apply this concept to a sample of 13 stars that host terrestrial planets similar to our Sun, utilising high-precision data on their elemental composition. Based on this and other constraints, we simulated the detailed mineral makeup of hypothetical Earth-like planets formed in a given star system. Analyzing the examples, we found that most of these planets would have compositions consisting of over 30% carborundum by volume, which could have profound implications for their structures and dynamics. Nevertheless, CSI is often subject to constraints such as limited measurements, noise, and regularization. Nevertheless, evaluating the accuracy of NN-based predictions proves more complicated than traditional methods. This difficulty arises from not only the random fluctuations inherent to noisy data but also limitations imposed by data quantity, model specifications, hyperparameters, optimization techniques, sampling, and overfitting. Despite some recent efforts to quantify uncertainty within NNs, no overarching framework effectively addresses uncertainty quantification even in relatively simple cases such as function approximation. Moreover, very little research has focused on solving partial differential equations and mapping infinite-dimensional functions using NNs. In this work, a unified framework encompassing uncertainty modeling, diverse solution approaches, performance metrics, and improvement techniques is introduced. To verify the utility and dependability of this framework, numerous methods are rigorously tested against benchmark problems featuring varied input and output data types, high-dimensional stochastic scenarios, and mixed problem types. Further details on all employed uncertainty quantification methods can be found in the appended description and are freely accessible through an open-source code library included with the framework.

(2019). Our paper focuses on the development of new algorithms for learning robust models, where the learner has more flexibility due to the use of local queries. We create the first distribution-free algorithms for achieving robust empirical risk minimization (ERM), a robust version of traditional ERM. Our first learning model utilizes local membership queries (LMQs), where the learner can obtain labeled versions of any input within a certain metric radius of a given point. We show that LMQs can be used to derive sample complexity bounds that approach those of active learning. Our second learning model utilizes more powerful local property queries (LPQs), where the learner can obtain information about any input within a certain metric radius by paying a constant amplitude. We show that LPQs allow us to achieve stronger robustness guarantees than LMQs, where the learner can achieve perfect robust ERM accuracy. We developed a new partition-based approach to tackle this problem, which involves dividing the data into neighborhoods based on the query information and optimizing the model separately for each area. We show that our method provides strong robustness guarantees and demonstrated its effectiveness through experiments using the MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets.

semiconductors, exemplified by the study of CrI$_3$, have generated significant enthusiasm due to their intriguing spin-dependent properties and their potential to revolutionize spintronics and magneto-optoelectronics. Through advanced theoretical calculations, researchers investigated the behavior of spin polarization within the prototype ferromagnetic CrI$_3$ bilayer, which has an in-plane magnetization orientation. Their investigation reveals that this ferromagnetic bilayer displays a rich pattern of spin texture within its uppermost valence bands, which arises from two unique spin cants resulting from the interplay of ferromagnetic order with both chirality and electrical polarization. One type of cant is a result of layer stacking asymmetry and valence state polarization, resulting in equivalent canting patterns on both layers. Conversely, the other cant is a consequence of Rashba effect, which in this ferromagnetic case generates oppositely canting components on adjacent layers within the same electronic state. Additionally, researchers formulated a set of rules governing spin polarization behavior within magnetic crystals based on their magnetic symmetry properties. Lastly, they found that applying compressive strain could effectively control the shape of spin texture within ferromagnetic CrI$_3$ bilayers by creating valence-band states with spins that can be aligned.

This method can learn a common representation using contrastive divergence and is applied to classification, information retrieval, and other related tasks. A significant drawback of traditional two-fan deep Boltzmann machine models lies in their inability to handle complex tasks effectively, particularly when multiple input modalities are incomplete or missing. We present a K-fan deep model, where the positive and negative branches are divided into K groups, with the number of groups determined automatically using the K-means algorithm. This method decomposes the joint distribution of multiple input sources into a product of marginal distributions and conditional distribution, which enables it to handle task-related missing or incomplete modalities more effectively. A deep belief learning method based on the K-fan deep model is employed to classify incomplete images and videos efficiently. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach in handling multiple incomplete modalities.

in validating the correctness of multi-threaded programs. Traditional unit and functional tests are insufficient due to the hidden nature of race conditions, which can evade detection by these tests. The McMini model checker, which is based on DPOR, has been expanded with a mechanism that enables the declaration of novel, fundamental thread operations through C code. The mechanism allows end-users to define their own thread activation policies, including the handling of spurious wake-ups triggered by condition variables. By specifying (i) when operations are allowed, (ii) which thread operations are mutually independent, and (iii) the overall program invariants, users can define their own customized thread activation policies. Additionally, users can define custom wake-up handlers to address problems related to wait operations, such as waiting for locks, semaphores, or custom handlers, which were previously unsupported, including cases involving spurious wake-ups. The McMini model checker has been successfully applied to various classic multi-threaded benchmark programs, including programs that utilize locks, semaphores, and custom handlers. The examples demonstrate their specification through the new declaration mechanism, and present the resulting models that can be verified using McMini. Furthermore, the examples also showcase their model checking performance, which has been found to include the model checking of programs that were previously impossible to verify.

Exploring the cosmic applications of supergravity provides a platform to investigate the potential outcomes of this theoretical framework, which could serve as the low-energy effective theory of superstrings-a potential quantum gravity candidate.  Developing inflationary models in supergravity, however, poses significant challenges stemming primarily from the constraints on scalar potentials and complicated interactions within the framework, as well as the excess degrees of freedom.  Addressing these issues requires navigating the constraints on desirable inflationary paths, moduli stabilization to achieve a stable de-Sitter phase, and ensuring the scalars remain heavy compared to the Hubble scale to facilitate single-field inflation.  Additionally, supergravity predicts several non-renormalizable interactions, rendering it an effective field theory that remains valid up to a specific cutoff energy scale, and thus necessitates a re-examination of the scalar potentials and field dynamics to achieve self-consistency at the quantum level. Their variation of the Bloomier filter can serve approximate membership queries efficiently, though no comprehensive testing of it exists to date. A different filter was developed, the xor filter, as an implementation of their idea, offering more effective efficiency and speeds. Notably, the developed xor filter can surpass both Bloom and cuckoo filters in performance, all while consuming a fraction of the storage space. A compact variant of the xor filter was also designed (xor+), resulting in storage needs similar to or smaller than already compressed sequences while providing similar speeds to membership testing. These new filters can serve as useful tools in preventing unnecessary actions and managing memory. They are most useful in scenarios where their storage and processing efficiency can provide notable enhancements over traditional Bloom and cuckoo filters. For instance, such scenarios include membership queries in distributed systems, file systems, caches, and networks, among others, where their data structures can easily be integrated and provide notable performance improvements.

urIPS 2021 - AWS Deepracer challenge, which required developing a self-driving vehicle model that interacts with its environment through action-reward interactions. The objective was to create an autonomous vehicle model that navigates a simulated track, adapts to real-world settings, and completes a lap at maximum speed while staying on course. The competition was part of The AI Driving Olympics (AI-DO), a series that fosters embodied cognition research through driving challenges, hosted by The AI-DO committee with support from The TF-Brain team. The Deepracer challenge proved to be a demanding task due to its intricate environment, limited availability of episode data, and the presence of noise in observation data. To overcome these challenges, we employed a combination of reinforcement learning (RL) techniques in a simulated environment. We leveraged model-based RL for policy development, integrating it with actor-critic methods that train a dynamic policy and adventure guided path planning for optimal navigation. When the episode data became usable around 5K iterations, we fine-tuned a deep Q-network (DQN) to optimize policy. Additionally, we conducted various experiments to validate the robustness of our solution across different environments. The final model demonstrated exceptional performance on both simulated and real-world vehicles, earning us the top spot in the competition.

Characterizing the masses of these envelopes in planets larger than Earth, especially those with masses of 1.7 to 3.5 Earth masses, remains a challenge to assessing their habitability potential. We demonstrate that observable differences exist between the solubility equilibria and thermochemistry of carbon and nitrogen gases in small vs. massive H2 atmospheres, with the requirement for a liquid water ocean and thermal equilibrium being inherently conflicting. Thermochemical recycling of carbon and nitrogen in the massive atmosphere of a temperate exoplanet typically produces CH4 and NH3, while a small atmosphere atop a liquid water ocean would contain CO2 and N2, with the presence of photochemically produced CO and CH4, and reduced NH3 due to dissolution in the ocean. These distinctive atmospheric compositions produce distinctive features in the planet's transmission spectrum, and multiple observations with the James Webb Space Telescope should enable differentiation between a small vs. massive atmosphere on temperate sub-Neptune exoplanets, including K2-18b, thereby facilitating a means to use current technology to estimate the mass of these atmospheres and assess their habitability potential.

2022 Out-Of-Vocabulary (OOV) challenge.
The competition highlighted an underinvestigated area in Optical Character Recognition (OCR) technology: accurately reading previously unseen text in real-world images during model training.
The dataset compiled for the competition comprises a diverse collection of 326,385 images, encompassing 4,864,405 text instances.
To address the challenge, a distinct validation and test set was created, comprising scene text that was not present in the training data.
The competition featured two recognition tasks: a holistic approach to reading full text and a focused task involving cropped text segments.
The analysis of baseline models and those submitted by competitors revealed a significant disparity between their performance levels in the newly introduced setting.
The proposed dataset will play a crucial role in further research to enhance the development of more versatile scene text models capable of providing more reliable and robust predictions.

Furthermore, attempting to utilize each individual sensor's measurement independently can be problematic due to their shared sources of error and varying signal strengths. This paper proposes a novel method called Partially-observed Individual Sensor EM (POISEM) that addresses these issues by utilizing a probabilistic approach to identify individual sensor trends beyond common correlations. Our approach involves two key components - first, it recognizes when and how long each sensor's readings are unfaithfully representative of their underlying trend, and second, it utilizes a modified EM algorithm to model the trend of each sensor based on this understanding. Our results show that POISEM outperforms existing methods in predicting trends for high-dimensional data collected from multiple industrial sensors.

Neural Networks (CNNs) are emerging due to rising demands for accurate predictions and thorough analyses. However, they necessitate a considerable amount of computational power and time for processing. Previous studies on pruning have focused on enhancing inference efficiency, but there's been limited research on effectively decreasing training costs. Our proposed framework, ClickTrain, efficiently and accurately enables end-to-end training of large CNNs on limited resources, focusing on both accuracy and inference speed. ClickTrain uses a two-stage process: an initial coarse-stage where a base model is trained on a reduced dataset with a simplified loss function, followed by a fine-stage where the model is precisely trained on the full dataset with the standard loss function. Additionally, ClickTrain employs a novel method called ClickForward to introduce sparsity during the training process, leveraging gradient information to identify and eliminate unessential parameters. Experimental results on multiple datasets across three fields have shown that ClickTrain can significantly reduce training time by 2-23 times while maintaining comparable accuracy and achieving significant speedups in inference, outperforming existing pruning methods and models.

When applied to Virgo data, our approach successfully recovers well-known neutron star and binary neutron star events from over 38,000 hours of joint LIGO-Virgo observations. Our approach's use of multi-dimensional gravitational wave parameters enhances its effectiveness in distinguishing neutron star and black hole merger signals from various sources of background noise. giant exoplanet, which orbits around a star called TOI-5542 approximately every 75 days. Initially detected by the TESS satellite, the exoplanet, which has a radius similar to that of Jupiter, has been further confirmed using data from ground-based spectrographic equipment. Analysis of this data has shown that the exoplanet, which has an estimated mass roughly equivalent to that of Jupiter, likely formed through migration or by remaining in its original location rather than being formed by a specific high-energy migration mechanism. Further study found that the host star, which is approximately 10 billion years old, has a metal composition that deviates from a common trend of metal-rich giant planets being formed around metal-rich host stars. Interestingly, this finding suggests that metal abundance may not be the primary factor in the formation of short-period giant exoplanets.

Two main obstacles arise when attempting to solve CMDPs for the development of optimal operational strategies: they are often characterized by a vast number of states and actions, as well as a multitude of constraints. Two current multi-timescale deep reinforcement learning methods used for tackling CMDPs - the advantage-based actor-critic method and the state-action advantage-based actor-critic method - are examined in this study. The study establishes their theoretical counterparts, proves their off-policy correctness, and provides a theoretical framework for their convergence. This framework is then supported by numerical simulations of a supply chain problem.

Unlike non-clustered networks, the presence of robust community structures in the network tends to cause a secondary outbreak of infections, resulting in two distinct periods of variability. To address these shortcomings, our approach integrates the actor-critic model with Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) for a hybrid framework termed the Hamiltonian Policy. Traditional offline data solutions often result in sub-optimal policies when the coverage condition isn't met, which frequently occurs with offline data. The pessimism principle resolves this problem by limiting actions with little state-dependent data usage. Although most pessimism-based methods depend on a key hyperparameter for pessimism quantification, their effectiveness is largely dependent on this parameter's proper choice. Our approach integrates the pessimism principle with Bayesian machine learning, using Thompson sampling to optimise the pessimism degree without manual adjustment. By developing a credible set with an optimistically bounded Q-function boundary, the need for additional pessimism parameter tuning is eliminated. Our general Bayesian learning method can accommodate a range of models, including Bayesian linear and neural network models. Additionally, a variational inference algorithm is developed for efficient and scalable computations. The proposed solutions' performance in creating robust and adaptable treatment policies is demonstrated through simulations and a real-world healthcare study.

These data types commonly appear in research contexts such as ecological studies, genetic information, and linguistic analyses examining word occurrences in texts. Clustering methods can effectively apply to this data for a range of purposes including the identification of geographically linked species groups, known as biotic elements. Various clustering approaches can be utilized to process such data including the use of latent class mixtures under the assumption of local independence, this study however focuses on density-based clustering methods utilizing the proximity of species' presence across different locations. Under local spatial contiguity, these density-based clusters are shown to have specific properties and an approach developed to increase the cluster's spatial consistency while maintaining independence across clusters. A well-known challenge with such clustering methods is determining the optimal number of clusters. This study proposes a method employing the multi-profiled Chinese restaurant process to assign locations to clusters and estimates the optimal number of clusters by fitting this model under different numbers of clusters and selecting the fit that maximizes the integrated clustering coherence. A method for quantifying the coherence of each location's assignment to a cluster is calculated as the maximum coherence among all possible cluster coherences and this study proposes two methods for improving cluster coherences, these being the Coherence Constrained Clustering method and the Conformance Constrained Clustering method. deep neural networks has received significant attention, but dealing with RGB and RGB-D images separately often necessitates the design of specific network architectures. This paper proposes an efficient and unified structure that integrates cross-attention context extraction to effectively tackle both tasks. By effectively fusing two inputs (for RGB images) or three inputs (for RGB-D images) with a cross-attention mechanism, our framework leverages the rich information present in both RGB and depth features. 2019 SemEval OffensEval Task is the subject of this paper. We adopted a dual-strategy to detect and classify hate speech in social media posts. Meanwhile, in subtasks B and C, a linear support vector machine was used in combination with pre-selected character n-gram features. Our method specifically for subtask C demonstrated effectiveness in identifying the victim of abusive content with a macro F1 score of 0.5243, and ranked 27th out of 65 participants.

Since most X-ray sources emit X-rays of multiple energy levels, which vary in their absorption rates, the process of reconstructing images typically involves a reverse ray transformation process. , has historically been challenging for object-oriented programming due to inefficiencies in memory allocation and access.  Despite this limitation, a range of applications, including real-world programs with inherent object structures, have been overlooked for parallelization opportunities.  Our research identified a particular subset of object-oriented programming called Single-Method Multiple-Objects (SMMO), which can be efficiently parallelized on SIMD devices by executing the same method across multiple objects of a given type.  To facilitate easy adoption of high-speed GPU programming for average developers, we created the DynaSOAr CPU+GPU framework, which automatically generates high-speed GPU code from serial code snippets that follow the SMMO pattern.  This framework exploits multiple hardware accelerators, including GPUs and CPUS, by simultaneously executing multiple instances of the parallelizable method call.  As a result, DynaSOAr allows any CPU-based SMMO program to be speedily ported to multiple hardware accelerators with a minimal two-line code transformation, while also supporting the development of new high-performance GPU microkernels through a simple and straightforward programming approach.  In conjunction with this framework, we developed a range of performance analysis and micro-kernel optimization tools that uncover and harvest potential parallelism in arbitrary C code, which leads to unexpected new application areas for high-performance GPU programming at both developer and algorithmic levels.

In optical applications, a common form of entanglement known as polarization entanglement typically arises from postselection methods, which are accompanied by destructive photon detection, limiting their usability in various applications. In this research, a new strategy is proposed to create entangled states of polarized photons without requiring postselection, instead opting for a heralded approach that ensures ready availability of entangled resources. By applying the quantum scissors technique to manipulate a specific type of entanglement known as continuous-variable entanglement, it is possible to create the desired hybrid entangled states, which are a combination of both discrete and continuous variables. We present two methods of implementing this technique, each utilizing a different technique to create the desired polarization entangled states: the first method incorporates a specific type of optical device known as a fiber-based device and the second utilizes a different type of optical device known as a bulk optical device. By analyzing the results of experimental simulations, it is clear that this method is capable of creating high-quality polarization entanglement, with superior results obtained from the bulk optical device approach. By further modifying the method, it is possible to create another form of entanglement known as dendritic entanglement, which is shown to have numerous benefits, such as reduced error rates and the ability to create more complex entangled states.

A graph has the PH-property if for each pairing of K_G, it shares a perfect matching that, when combined, creates a Hamiltonian cycle of K_G. Cubic graphs that possess the PH-property have been fully characterized, with a recent theorem stating their Hamiltonian cycle problem is NP-complete. This characterization includes a convenient syndrome test to identify whether a given pairing's combined matching forms a Hamiltonian cycle of K_G. Building on this, we introduce a generalized syndrome test that can be applied to any graph of odd order with a perfect matching, effectively expanding the PH-property's scope. A new family of graphs that possess this extended PH-property and have chromatic index 3 is established, consisting of graphs obtained by replacing a vertex of a complete graph of odd order with its complete bipartite counterpart.

a significant transformation in the field of reversible steganography. A key foundation of reversible steganography relies on predictive modeling that can be achieved using deep neural networks. However, critical inaccuracies persist when dealing with data outside the scope of a model's training and noisy data. To address this challenge, we introduce the concept of uncertainty in predictive models rooted in the theoretical framework of Bayesian deep learning. Bayesian neural networks are essentially intelligent systems that recognize their own shortcomings. To accurately quantify uncertainty, we approximate the posterior predictive distribution by leveraging Monte Carlo sampling combined with stochastic forward passes. Furthermore, we demonstrate that predictive uncertainty can be separated into aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties, both of which can be learned through unsupervised methods. Experimental findings show that the application of Bayesian uncertainty analysis results in improved steganographic performance with regard to capacity-distortion metrics.

The findings reveal a uniform distribution of magnetic bright points in the observed region, with their area sizes ranging from 0.08 to 0.8 times the area of a typical pixel, and their peak brightness levels varying between 180 and 1800 times the brightness of a typical pixel. The area size and brightness of magnetic bright points exhibited correlations, with their area sizes increasing and brightness levels decreasing as the magnetic flux increases. The observed area size and brightness of magnetic bright points are consistent with independent estimates of their properties, obtained using the magnetic flux and albedo values from the HSRA synoptic map. The calculated area size and brightness of magnetic bright points are found to be in agreement with the predictions based on a model, assuming a uniform background brightness level and magnetic field strength. The model suggests that the magnetic bright points' properties would remain unchanged if they occupied one percent of the solar photosphere's area. The high-resolution observations of magnetic bright points can be used to calculate the solar plasma's temperature and density,

we examine electromagnetic and gravitational waves emitted during a process where a white dwarf loses mass to a black hole through tidal forces. A prominent challenge lies in resolving the isomorphism problem for bounded-degree graphs, a decision problem that falls within PTIME but remains unresolved. A promising method for addressing this issue involves utilizing a characterization of PTIME via first-order logic with a limited number of variables. Research has established that CPT's logic capabilities are equivalent to that of (generalized) distance-based first-order logic (DBFOL). A key constraint of DBFOL is its reliance on a fixed maximum distance between variables in formulas, a restriction that appears to be essential for resolving the isomorphism problem. This limitation is further examined by exploring two decision problems for bounded-degree graphs: verifying whether a graph's vertex color class includes two elements and determining if a graph's vertex subcomponent is a path. Although these problems can be solved using CPT, their definitions inherently include unbounded distances between variables, rendering them unsolvable using DBFOL. A crucial insight emerges from this investigation: a decision problem that falls within PTIME may not be solvable using CPT, suggesting that CPT might be too powerful for tackling decision problems with a reasonable number of variables. Yet, data sets generated from scientific endeavors often comprise vast 3D data volumes characterized by significant portions of zeroes, non-uniform distribution of values, and high generation rates. To handle the collapse of the traditional Q-function in continuous time, we derive a first-order approximation and introduce the term "small q-function". The q-function has connections to both the instantaneous advantage rate function and the Hamiltonian. We develop a continuous-time "Q-learning" framework based on the q-function, separate from time discretization, by characterizing its relationship to value functions and stochastic processes via martingale conditions. We apply this theory to create actor-critic algorithms for solving reinforcement learning tasks, either when or not the Gibbs measure density can be calculated. Our algorithms either relate to SARSA, recover Jia and Zhou's policy gradient algorithm, or provide alternative options. We validate the efficacy of these algorithms via simulation experiments, comparing them to Jia and Zhou's policy gradient algorithm and conventional time-discretized Q-learning algorithms.

The flow rates of physical processes are calculated from the anti-symmetric transition measures defined on the network of states. The statistical mechanics approach to thermodynamics relies on these flow rates to derive state function equations, but typically assumes that the system is in long-term steady-state. Our work generalizes this concept to transient systems by integrating the flow rates into the relative entropy. This allows us to derive a compact equation for relative entropy's derivative and, through repeated application, the flow rate's partial derivative. The success of this method is demonstrated by successfully adapting it to already existing models. The outcomes show that the relative entropy formula can be used to determine the flow rate formula, and vice versa. The validity of our method is confirmed by obtaining the flow rate from the relative entropy, which, when used to establish a flow rate gradient, perfectly matches the original model's flow rate formula. The apparent difference between our approach and existing methods stems from the use of the relative entropy rather than the probability distribution. To overcome this limitation, we have shown that our results can also be expressed in terms of the probability distribution. Consequently, the proposed method is compatible with the traditional statistical mechanics approach.

influence on science by suggesting that he struggled with mathematical proficiency. This perceived weakness drove him to focus on experimentation and empiricism, as well as embracing the telescope's capabilities. His emphasis on hands-on research, which is often credited as an innovative aspect of his scientific approach, might actually be a consequence of his inability to make meaningful mathematical contributions. Similarly, his extensive use of mathematical tools held a different significance: it served as a means of communicating his ideas to those with a basic understanding of mathematics, such as the Duke's family, or as a demonstration of his expertise to his academic peers. In essence, Galileo's scientific legacy was shaped by both his scientific discoveries and his ability to present complex ideas in a universally accessible format.

Our study focuses on examining non-Gaussian influences on Saha's ionization through the application of Tsallis statistics. We addressed this challenge by generalizing the number density with a non-Gaussian distribution based on Fermi-Dirac theory and then formulated the Saha equation for cosmological abundance. Our analysis reveals that under the influence of non-Gaussian potentials, Tsallis' thermodynamic framework tends to produce less restrictive conditions for matter domination. Additionally, our results indicate that ultra-light dark particles could emerge as a viable option to resolve the Hubble tension, which emerges as a notable finding from our study. Moreover, we have expanded upon the conventional criteria for matter domination by including the impact of anisotropic pressure for diverse fluid types. This has led to the discovery of more stringent constraints for certain dark energy models, which were previously overlooked. Our research utilizes a Bayesian analysis to incorporate data from Hubble and Shaw, as well as Planck cosmic microwave background observations.
